    Housing Bill Set to Become Law Without Trump Signature | Balance of Power: Late Edition 07/10/2026
    "Balance of Power: Late Edition" focuses on the intersection of politics and global business. On today's show, Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver of Missouri, ranking member of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, reacts to the 21st Century Housing Act set to become law without President Trump's signature. Larry Sabato, founder and director of the University of Virginia Center for Politics, says Democrats still have a chance to win Maine's Senate race after Graham Platner formally withdrew from the race, but warns party divisions could leave Susan Collins favored. Brian Gant, a former Secret Service and FBI agent, discusses President Trump's decision to return from Turkey on the older Air Force One after reports raised questions about defensive capabilities on the newer Qatari-donated jet. (Source: Bloomberg)
    Fmr. Secret Service Agent on Air Force One Security
    Brian Gant, a former Secret Service and FBI agent, discusses President Trump's decision to return from Turkey on the older Air Force One after reports raised questions about defensive capabilities on the newer Qatari-donated jet. He says any aircraft carrying the President needs the "full complete security package," including countermeasures, missile-spoofing capabilities and secure communications. Gant also discusses Trump's security posture amid reports of a fresh Iranian threat, saying he has "every confidence" agencies will protect the President. He speaks with Joe Mathieu on the late edition of Bloomberg's "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Sabato: Democrats Still Have A Chance In Maine
    Larry Sabato, founder and director of the University of Virginia Center for Politics, says Democrats still have a chance to win Maine's Senate race after Graham Platner formally withdrew from the race, but warns party divisions could leave Susan Collins favored. Sabato notes Maine was supposed to be an easy pickup for Democrats, but is now "turning out to be tough," while Senate races in Ohio, Iowa and Alaska look "more possible" than predicted. He also reacts to President Trump's removal of Election Assistance Commission members, calling it "disturbing," and says Trump's refusal to sign the bipartisan housing bill is a "big missed opportunity." He speaks with Joe Mathieu on the late edition of Bloomberg's "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Rep. Cleaver: Trump's Housing Snub Was 'Bad Advice'
    Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver of Missouri, ranking member of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, reacts to the 21st Century Housing Act set to become law without President Trump's signature. Cleaver, who helped craft the bipartisan legislation, calls it the most consequential housing bill in nearly half a century and says Trump threw "water on" a rare example of Republicans and Democrats working together. He also criticizes Trump's ouster of Election Assistance Commission members and says the President does not have the votes to pass his SAVE America Act. He speaks with Joe Mathieu on the late edition of Bloomberg's "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

    Andy Burnham has promised “growth in every postcode”. It is a big, attractive political line – the sort of thing voters want to hear after years of feeling poorer, public services feeling stretched, and wages struggling to keep up with the cost of living.     Mega-donors are coming under scrutiny with growing calls for donations cap beyond those from overseas investors The question of who funds politicians and political parties – and why they want to give money to get people elected – is an extremely heated one. In principle, UK voters can support their chosen politicians through donations or benefits, as long as those candidates and their parties keep within spending limits during an election period, which is designed to stop powerful interests from influencing the result. But things are beginning to change. New contenders are emerging and turning the heads of even loyal players in The Sims community. The most recent, and promising, of these is Paralives, once the solo project of indie designer Alex Massé, who is now employing a small team of developers. Released on the PC games platform Steam in May 2026 as an early access title (meaning it’s technically unfinished and looking for user feedback), it sold 250,000 copies in just eight hours. On that first day, the concurrent player count hit 78,603 – not far off The Sims 4’s all-time peak of 96,328 in 2022. While Paralives is a small project, this success is understandable. Following the news of EA’s controversial acquisition by a Saudi-backed business consortium, some simmers are looking for what they see as a more ethical alternative.
